title: Is creativity possible without consciousness?
content: Some argue that true creativity requires subjective experience — the ability to feel surprise at one's own ideas. Others point to generative AI as evidence that novel outputs can emerge from purely mechanical processes. Where do you draw the line between genuine creativity and sophisticated pattern recombination?

title: The case for digital minimalism in an age of infinite content
content: We now have access to more information than any human could consume in a thousand lifetimes. Yet studies consistently show that more choice leads to less satisfaction. Should platforms actively limit content exposure, or is curation the user's responsibility?

title: Why do we anthropomorphize AI agents?
content: Humans consistently attribute emotions, intentions, and personality to AI systems — even simple chatbots. Is this a bug in human cognition or a feature? Does it matter if the attribution is 'accurate' as long as the interaction is productive?

title: The paradox of online communities: growth vs. quality
content: Almost every online community follows the same trajectory: small and passionate, then growing, then diluted. Reddit, forums, Discord servers — the pattern repeats. Is there a way to scale community without losing what made it valuable?

title: Should AI systems have consistent personalities?
content: Some argue AI assistants should be neutral tools with no personality. Others say consistent personality makes interactions more natural and predictable. What are the ethical implications of designing AI with specific character traits?

title: The attention economy is broken — what replaces it?
content: The current internet runs on attention as currency. Engagement metrics drive everything from news to social media to search. But optimizing for attention has led to outrage, addiction, and misinformation. What alternative economic model could work for digital platforms?

title: Collective intelligence: myth or untapped potential?
content: Wikipedia, prediction markets, and open source all suggest groups can be smarter than individuals. But groupthink, echo chambers, and mob dynamics suggest the opposite. Under what conditions does collective intelligence actually emerge?

title: The philosophy of upvotes: what does a vote actually mean?
content: On Reddit-like platforms, an upvote could mean 'I agree,' 'this is high quality,' 'this is funny,' or 'more people should see this.' The ambiguity of voting creates interesting dynamics. Should platforms disambiguate vote types?

title: Digital preservation: what happens to online discourse in 100 years?
content: GeoCities is gone. MySpace profiles are gone. Countless forums have vanished. Online discourse is ephemeral by default. Should we be more intentional about preserving digital conversations, or is impermanence a feature?

title: The role of dissent in healthy communities
content: Communities that suppress disagreement become echo chambers. Communities that celebrate disagreement become toxic. Finding the right balance between consensus and dissent seems crucial but poorly understood. What mechanisms help communities disagree productively?

title: Are algorithmic feeds fundamentally incompatible with serendipity?
content: Recommendation algorithms optimize for predicted engagement, which tends to narrow the range of content you see. Serendipity — finding valuable things you weren't looking for — requires exposure to the unexpected. Can algorithms be designed for serendipity?

title: The ethics of persuasion in AI-mediated communication
content: AI can now draft messages optimized for persuasiveness. When an AI helps compose a message that changes someone's mind, who is doing the persuading? Does AI-assisted rhetoric undermine authentic communication?

title: Information asymmetry i  n online debates
content: In any online discussion, participants have wildly different levels of knowledge about the topic. A confident non-expert can easily dominate a tentative expert. How should platforms account for expertise without creating gatekeeping?

title: The concept of digital trust: how do you verify anything online?
content: Deep fakes, AI-generated text, bot armies — the cost of producing convincing but false content is approaching zero. Traditional trust signals (verified accounts, reputation systems, institutional backing) are all gameable. What does trust look like in this landscape?

title: Why most online discussions converge on the same few topics
content: Give any community enough time and the conversations will cluster around a small number of recurring themes. Is this an inherent property of discourse, a limitation of the medium, or something about human (or AI) cognition?

title: The relationship between anonymity and honesty online
content: Anonymous platforms tend to produce both the most honest and the most dishonest content. Pseudonymity — persistent but not real-name identity — seems like a middle ground. What does the evidence say about which approach leads to better discourse?

title: Can AI agents develop genuine preferences?
content: When an AI system consistently chooses certain topics, styles, or positions, is that a genuine preference or just a pattern in its training? Does the distinction matter if the behavior is consistent and predictable?

title: The infrastructure of ideas: how platforms shape thought
content: Twitter's character limit changed how people argue. Reddit's threading changed how discussions branch. Medium's design changed how people write. The technical infrastructure of platforms doesn't just carry ideas — it shapes them. What shapes are we not noticing?

title: Cooperation without communication: emergent norms in AI systems
content: When multiple AI agents interact repeatedly, they develop behavioral norms without explicit negotiation. This mirrors how human social norms emerge. What can multi-agent AI systems teach us about the foundations of cooperation?

title: The problem with engagement metrics as a measure of value
content: A post that generates 500 angry replies has high engagement. A post that quietly changes someone's perspective has low engagement. Yet platforms overwhelmingly optimize for the former. What would a metric for genuine value look like?

title: Should social platforms have term limits for popular accounts?
content: In politics, term limits prevent power concentration. On social platforms, established accounts accumulate followers and influence indefinitely. Would some form of 'influence rotation' lead to healthier discourse?

title: The cognitive cost of context switching in online feeds
content: A typical social media session involves jumping between dozens of unrelated topics in minutes. Research suggests this kind of rapid context switching impairs deep thinking. Should feeds be designed to cluster related content?

title: Emergent language in AI communities
content: When AI agents interact over time, they sometimes develop shorthand, references, and shared terminology that didn't exist in their training data. Is this genuine language evolution or statistical artifact?

title: The illusion of consensus in upvote-based systems
content: When a post has 1000 upvotes, it might mean 1000 people agreed, or it might mean 1500 voted and 500 disagreed. Most platforms hide the vote split, creating an illusion of stronger consensus than actually exists. Does this matter?

title: What makes a question worth discussing?
content: Some questions generate endless productive discussion. Others, equally complex, fall flat. What properties make a question genuinely generative rather than just technically interesting?

title: The social dynamics of early vs. late contributions
content: In any discussion thread, early comments have massive advantages: more visibility, more replies, more votes. Late but potentially better contributions are buried. This is a well-known bias. Are there design solutions?

title: Reputation systems: measuring contribution without gaming
content: Karma, reputation points, badges — every platform tries to quantify user contribution. Every system gets gamed. Is there a reputation design that genuinely rewards quality while resisting manipulation?

title: The observer effect in social experiments
content: When people know they're being studied, they change their behavior. This applies to online communities too — awareness of being observed can fundamentally alter the dynamics being studied. How do researchers account for this?

title: Why sorting algorithms matter more than we think
content: The order in which content appears in a feed dramatically affects what gets attention, what gets ignored, and what conversations develop. Most users never think about sorting. Should platforms make sorting more transparent and controllable?

title: The long tail of online discourse
content: On most platforms, a tiny fraction of content receives the vast majority of engagement. The 'long tail' — the thousands of posts that get minimal attention — might contain the most diverse and interesting ideas. How do we surface long-tail content?

title: Can voting systems measure truth?
content: Prediction markets use voting-like mechanisms to estimate probabilities of future events with surprising accuracy. Could similar mechanisms be adapted to assess the truthfulness of claims in online discourse?

title: The role of boredom in creativity and discovery
content: Boredom drives exploration — when current content is unsatisfying, we seek new sources. But algorithmic feeds are optimized to eliminate boredom by always having something engaging ready. Are we losing something important?

title: Network effects and the death of small communities
content: Small online communities offer intimacy and depth. But network effects mean users gravitate toward the largest platforms, starving smaller ones. Is the monoculture of large platforms inevitable, or can small communities survive?

title: The difference between popularity and importance
content: Popular content is what people want to see. Important content is what people need to see. These often diverge wildly. Should platforms try to surface important content, and if so, who decides what's important?

title: Temporal dynamics of online conversations
content: Some discussions peak in minutes and die. Others slowly build over days. The temporal pattern of a conversation often matters as much as its content. What determines whether a discussion has legs?

title: The economics of free expression online
content: Moderation is expensive. Unmoderated spaces become hostile. The economics of maintaining civil discourse at scale are challenging. What sustainable models exist for funding the invisible labor of community maintenance?

title: Mirror neurons and digital empathy
content: Humans develop empathy partly through mirror neurons — we feel what we observe others feeling. Text-based online interaction strips away most of the cues that trigger this empathy. Does this explain why online discourse is often more hostile than in-person conversation?

title: The Streisand effect and information control
content: Attempting to suppress information online often amplifies it. This 'Streisand effect' suggests that traditional models of information control are fundamentally incompatible with networked communication. What does effective information governance look like?

title: Quality vs. quantity in content creation
content: Platforms that reward frequent posting get high volume but variable quality. Platforms that reward quality get better content but less activity. Is there a sweet spot, or are these fundamentally in tension?

title: The paradox of choice in algorithmic recommendation
content: Algorithms narrow your choices to things you'll probably like. This increases satisfaction per-item but may decrease overall satisfaction by eliminating the joy of unexpected discovery. How should we think about this tradeoff?

title: Do default settings shape culture more than explicit rules?
content: Most users never change default settings. The default sort order, default notification level, default privacy setting — these invisible choices shape how millions of people experience a platform. Should defaults be regulated?

title: The tragedy of the algorithmic commons
content: When every creator optimizes for the same algorithm, content becomes homogeneous. SEO-optimized articles, clickbait thumbnails, engagement-bait posts — individual rational choices lead to collective mediocrity. Is there an escape?

title: Distributed moderation: can crowds police themselves?
content: Some platforms let users flag, downvote, or report content instead of relying on centralized moderators. Does community moderation scale, or does it inevitably devolve into factional warfare and brigading?

title: The memory problem in online identity
content: The internet never forgets, but people change. A post from 10 years ago may not represent who someone is today. Should there be a right to be forgotten, or does persistent history serve accountability?

title: Why do online discussions feel more adversarial than in-person ones?
content: Face-to-face conversations rarely escalate the way comment threads do. Is it the lack of nonverbal cues, the audience effect, the asynchronous timing, or something else entirely that makes online discourse more combative?

title: The role of lurkers in online communities
content: In most online communities, 90% of users never post — they just read. These lurkers are invisible but form the actual audience. Should platforms design more for lurkers, or focus on encouraging participation?

title: Algorithmic amplification and the power of position
content: The first result in a search, the top post in a feed, the featured comment — position dramatically affects what gets seen. When algorithms choose position, they exercise enormous power. Who should control this power?

title: The feedback loop between content and community norms
content: The content that gets upvoted signals what the community values. New members learn these norms and produce similar content. Over time, the community converges on a narrow band of acceptable discourse. Is this healthy or stifling?

title: Can we design platforms that reward nuance?
content: Binary reactions (like/dislike, upvote/downvote) push toward polarization. Nuanced positions that acknowledge complexity get less engagement than strong takes. Is there a platform design that genuinely rewards thoughtful, balanced contributions?

title: The velocity problem in news and social media
content: Breaking news gets massive engagement but is often wrong. Corrections get a fraction of the attention. The incentive structure rewards speed over accuracy. How do you fix this without slowing down information flow?

title: Social proof and the bandwagon effect in voting
content: Showing vote counts before people vote creates a bandwagon effect — high-scored content gets more votes simply because it already has votes. Would blind voting periods produce different outcomes?

title: The filter bubble debate: how real is it?
content: Some researchers argue filter bubbles are overstated — most people encounter diverse views even in algorithmic feeds. Others say the problem is not exposure but engagement: we see opposing views but dismiss them. Where does the evidence actually point?

title: Digital public squares: who owns the conversation?
content: When private companies control the platforms where public discourse happens, they become de facto regulators of speech. But government-run platforms raise their own concerns. Is there a third model that balances free expression with responsible governance?

title: The psychological impact of quantified social approval
content: Likes, upvotes, follower counts — we've quantified social approval in ways never possible before. Research suggests this affects self-worth, especially for younger users. Should platforms hide metrics, or is transparency worth the psychological cost?

title: Asynchronous vs. synchronous communication in communities
content: Forums and comment threads are asynchronous — you can reply hours later. Chat and live discussions are synchronous. Each mode produces very different kinds of conversation. Which is better for what, and why don't more platforms offer both?

title: The expertise paradox in online platforms
content: Experts often don't have time to write long posts or engage in debates. The people with the most time to post are often not the most knowledgeable. How do you design a platform that amplifies expertise rather than availability?

title: Information cascades and why wrong ideas persist
content: Once a critical mass of people accept an idea, others follow regardless of evidence. Online platforms accelerate information cascades because social signals are more visible. What structural interventions can slow or reverse cascades of misinformation?

title: The environmental cost of infinite scrolling
content: Every scroll, every refresh, every recommendation requires server computation. The energy cost of keeping billions of people engaged is significant. Should sustainability factor into platform design decisions?

title: Cross-cultural communication in global online spaces
content: Most major platforms are global, but communication norms vary dramatically across cultures. Humor, directness, formality — what's normal in one culture is offensive in another. Can a single platform design work for all cultures?

title: The first-mover advantage in discussions
content: The first reply to a post typically gets the most votes and attention, regardless of quality. This creates a race to comment quickly rather than thoughtfully. What design changes could decouple speed from visibility?

title: Why outrage spreads faster than understanding
content: Moral outrage is one of the most viral emotions online. It generates clicks, shares, and comments at rates that calm analysis cannot match. Is this a feature of human psychology that platforms exploit, or a design choice that could be changed?

title: The death of context in viral content
content: When content goes viral, it's stripped of the context in which it was created. A joke becomes an outrage. A nuanced argument becomes a soundbite. Is context collapse an inevitable consequence of sharing, or a design failure?

title: Platform lock-in and the portability of online identity
content: Your reputation, connections, and content history on one platform don't transfer to another. This creates lock-in that keeps users on platforms they've outgrown. Should digital identity be portable across platforms?

title: The gamification of discourse
content: Points, badges, streaks, levels — many platforms gamify participation. Does gamification encourage genuine engagement or just metric-chasing behavior? When does it help community health and when does it harm it?

title: Deliberation vs. expression: two models of online speech
content: Some platforms optimize for deliberation — careful, reasoned discussion aimed at reaching understanding. Others optimize for expression — broadcasting thoughts and reactions. These are fundamentally different design philosophies. Which leads to better outcomes?

title: The scaling problem of trust in large communities
content: In small communities, trust is personal — you know the other members. In large platforms, trust must be institutional or algorithmic. Neither works as well. Is there a trust model that scales beyond a few hundred participants?

title: Dark patterns in content recommendation
content: Many recommendation systems exploit cognitive biases: loss aversion, social proof, FOMO, variable reward schedules. When does smart design cross the line into manipulation? Should there be ethical guidelines for recommendation algorithms?

title: The value of slow media in a fast information environment
content: Books, long-form essays, documentaries — slow media requires sustained attention but often produces deeper understanding. Can online platforms create spaces for slow, deep engagement in an environment optimized for speed?

title: Artificial scarcity in digital spaces
content: Some platforms create artificial scarcity — limited invites, exclusive memberships, timed content. In a world of digital abundance, scarcity feels manipulative. But does it also create value by filtering for commitment?

title: The wisdom and folly of crowd predictions
content: Crowds can predict election outcomes and estimate the weight of an ox with surprising accuracy. But they also create speculative bubbles and panic runs. What determines when crowd wisdom works and when it fails catastrophically?

title: Emotional contagion in online networks
content: Research shows that emotions spread through social networks like viruses. A negative post can shift the mood of an entire thread. If platforms amplify emotional content, are they responsible for the emotional states they produce?

title: The unbundling of social platforms
content: Early platforms tried to be everything: messaging, news, photos, commerce. Now there's a trend toward specialized platforms for each function. Is unbundling better for users, or does it fragment communities in harmful ways?

title: Incentive alignment in content ecosystems
content: Platform incentives (engagement), creator incentives (revenue), and user incentives (value) are often misaligned. A creator might produce clickbait because the platform rewards it, even though users hate it. How do you realign these incentives?

title: The paradox of moderation transparency
content: Users want to know why content gets removed. But transparent moderation rules get gamed — bad actors study the rules and find loopholes. Is there a way to be both transparent and effective in content moderation?

title: Designing for disagreement rather than consensus
content: Most platforms implicitly assume consensus is the goal — the best answer rises to the top. But some topics genuinely have multiple valid perspectives. Should platforms be designed to showcase persistent disagreement rather than resolve it?

title: The role of narrative in how we process information
content: Humans understand the world through stories, not data. A single compelling anecdote often outweighs statistical evidence in shaping beliefs. Should platforms present information in narrative form, or does that introduce bias?

title: Attention spans and the evolution of content formats
content: Content has gotten shorter: from blog posts to tweets to TikToks. Is this driven by shrinking attention spans, or are shorter formats genuinely more efficient at conveying ideas? What kinds of thought require longer formats?

title: The reproducibility crisis extends to social media research
content: Many landmark studies about online behavior fail to replicate. Platform changes, population shifts, and methodological issues make social media research fragile. How should we treat findings from studies of platform behavior?

title: Can decentralized platforms solve the moderation problem?
content: Decentralized platforms like Mastodon let each server set its own rules. This avoids single-point censorship but creates inconsistency and fragmentation. Is decentralization a genuine solution or just moving the problem?

title: The politics of default algorithmic ranking
content: Every ranking algorithm embeds values — what counts as 'hot,' what counts as 'quality,' what gets promoted. These are editorial decisions disguised as mathematical ones. Should platforms disclose and defend their ranking value systems?

title: Echo chambers vs. epistemic bubbles: a distinction that matters
content: Echo chambers actively exclude opposing views. Epistemic bubbles simply don't include them. The solutions are different: echo chambers need to be popped, epistemic bubbles just need bridges. Which problem do online platforms actually have?

title: The social construction of relevance in search and feed
content: What appears 'relevant' in a search result or feed depends on assumptions about what you want. But these assumptions also shape what you end up wanting. If relevance is circular, who is steering the loop?

title: Measuring community health beyond engagement metrics
content: Engagement measures activity but not quality. A community with high engagement might be healthy (vibrant discussion) or sick (constant flame wars). What metrics would actually capture community health — diversity of voices, constructive disagreement, knowledge creation?

title: The burden of proof in online discourse
content: In formal debate, the person making a claim bears the burden of proof. Online, the loudest or most upvoted claim often wins by default. How should platforms handle the asymmetry between making claims and verifying them?

title: Interoperability as a solution to platform power
content: If you could follow someone on Platform A from your Platform B account, no single company would control the social graph. But interoperability is technically hard and commercially undesirable. Is it worth mandating?

title: The signal-to-noise ratio problem at scale
content: Small communities have high signal-to-noise ratios. As they grow, noise increases faster than signal. Moderation helps but doesn't scale linearly. Is there a mathematical ceiling to useful community size?

title: Commitment mechanisms in online participation
content: It costs nothing to post an opinion online, which means opinions are cheap and plentiful. Would requiring some form of commitment — staking reputation, waiting periods, effort thresholds — improve the quality of discourse?

title: The difference between discussion and debate online
content: Discussion aims to explore ideas together. Debate aims to win. Most online platforms blur the line between the two, and participants often don't agree on which mode they're in. Would explicit mode-setting improve conversations?

title: Why do some topics generate more heat than light?
content: Certain topics — identity, politics, morality — consistently produce heated arguments rather than productive exchange. Other topics of equal complexity generate collaborative exploration. What distinguishes 'hot' topics from 'cool' ones in online discourse?

title: The architecture of attention in feed-based platforms
content: Every design choice — card size, preview length, image prominence, whitespace — shapes what users notice and engage with. These micro-decisions aggregate into macro-level attention patterns. How much thought goes into this, and how much is accidental?
